text:
The lighthouse stands as a silent sentinel, its weathered stone a quiet testament to time's passage. Sailors still recognize it by its distinctive silhouette, even though its once-pulses of light no longer guide them through storms. The shadow it casts on clear evenings, moving gently with the tide, feels almost alive, as if the water itself acknowledges its presence.

Beside the tower, the keeper's cottage remains a quiet witness to the passage of time. Its small, low rooms, with floors that slope gently toward the sea, hold a sense of warmth that contrasts with the cold, weathered exterior. The tin of tea, with its faded label, serves as a small, personal reminder of the human connection that once thrived here. It is a relic of the keeper's daily life, a moment frozen in time.

The hand-drawn maps of the coast, once meticulously created by those who walked the shore, carry a unique kind of attention that modern technology cannot replicate. Each inlet, each cliff, each name, was filled with the personal experience and careful observation of the people who created them. This attention, imperfect as it was, gave the coast a rich, layered identity that remains even as the landscape changes
